caseStudies.title: The build that was never green because it never ran
caseStudies.subtitle: How 28 red runs in a row turned out to be a billing decision, and what a local gate is actually for when the runner never starts

hero.headline: The pipeline went red because the bill was due.
hero.body: On 21 October 2026 the account this project lives on used the last of its 2,000 included Actions minutes, with eleven days of the month still to go. Twenty-eight runs out of the last thirty failed, and not one of them failed on code.

problem.headline: A red build is not always a red build
problem.body:
On 21 October 2026, the account running this workspace ran out of its included GitHub Actions minutes. The notification said it plainly:

> You have used 100% of the Actions minutes included for the omeiza-workspace account
>
> **2,000 min used / 2,000 min included**
>
> You'll be billed for usage beyond the included amount — unless a $0 budget is set for Actions, which blocks further usage until it resets. Your usage will reset in 11 days on November 01, 2026.

Eleven days of pipeline left to run, and no minutes to run it on. Every job from that point either cost money per minute or did not start at all.

The largest repository in the workspace, `bytesickle-web`, had **28 failing runs out of the last 30**. Every one failed in about six seconds, with the same annotation:

> The job was not started because recent account payments have failed or your spending limit needs to be increased. Please check the 'Billing & plans' section in your settings

The cause was the bill, not the code. The included minutes were gone, the spending limit that would have allowed paid overage had been reached, and the jobs were never allocated a runner at all.

Taken at face value a red build is a red build. The developer assumes their change broke something, and either fixes a problem that does not exist or pushes again and waits. What actually happened was that **nothing was verified at all**, and the reason was one line of text in a log nobody reads.

The failure was not a flake and it was not a regression. It was an infrastructure ceiling, and it looked exactly like a broken build — which is the part that makes it worth writing down.
problem.pullQuote: The pipeline went red because the bill was due. Twenty-eight runs in a row, and not one of them failed on code.
symptoms: 28 of the last 30 runs failed, none of them on code
Every failure arrived in about six seconds — far too fast for a test or a compile
The account's 2,000 included minutes were exhausted with 11 days left in the cycle
Until the reset on 1 November, every job either cost money per minute or did not start
A stale secret-scan allowlist entry and 93 dependency advisories, 8 of them critical, were waiting behind the same wall

approach.headline: Stop renting a runner to find out whether your code is broken
approach.body:
The fix is not to buy more minutes. It is to notice that most of what the pipeline does every single commit does not need a shared machine at all: the lint, the type check, the unit tests, and the workflow files themselves. Those can run on the laptop in front of the developer, in about a hundred seconds, for nothing.

CI Kit gives a repository a local gate that mirrors what the GitHub Actions workflow does: the same installs, the same linters, the same type checks, the same tests. The design principle is a single copy of the setup. The gate scripts live in the repository under `scripts/ci/`, and both the Makefile and the workflow call them. One copy of the setup, so it cannot disagree with itself.

That matters more than it sounds. The usual reason a local gate and a CI run disagree is that they are two implementations of the same intent that drift. Here they are the same files, so the only thing that can differ is the hardware.

The gates are driven by what the repository actually contains, so the tool works with any language rather than being one language's plugin. It also runs the workflow files themselves locally through `act`, so the YAML is checked before the push rather than after it.

For the eleven days until the reset, this was the difference between shipping and not shipping. The checks that no longer need a runner no longer need minutes, and the account's allowance stopped being the constraint on whether the work could move.

architecture.headline: Four parts

steps.title: The shared setup
steps.body: scripts/ci/*.sh holds every install and every gate. The Makefile calls them. The workflow calls them. There is no second implementation anywhere, so the local verdict and the CI verdict agree by construction rather than by luck.

steps.title: The gate targets
steps.body: make ci runs the full gate, make ci-fast runs lint and type checks only. The targets are generated from the repository's contents, so a TypeScript repository gets vue-tsc and a Go repository gets go vet, without configuration.

steps.title: make doctor
steps.body: A separate check for whether the local toolchain is the one CI pins. This is the diagnostic that tells you the two environments differ, before a failing test makes you guess.

steps.title: make act
steps.body: Runs the GitHub Actions workflow files locally through act, so the YAML itself is validated on the laptop. A malformed workflow is caught before it is pushed, not after it is queued.

diagram: |   the same script, so the local run and the runner
|   cannot disagree about what the code needs        |

results.headline: The honest measurement, including the part that is not a win

before.metric: Feedback on a push that breaks the build
Feedback when the runner never starts
before.value: 6 s, if you read the log

before.metric: Feedback when the runner never starts and you are not reading the log
Commits verified during a billing block

after.metric: Feedback on a push that breaks the build
Feedback when the runner never starts
Feedback when the runner never starts and you are not reading the log
Commits verified during a billing block

notes: The local gate is not faster than a CI runner. On identical work — npm ci, two type checks, vitest, the build — it measured 99 s on a 2022 Intel laptop against 43–48 s on a GitHub runner. A modern runner has more cores and faster storage, and for work that is mostly npm ci and TypeScript, it wins. The local gate on that machine is roughly twice the wall clock.

The first attempt at that measurement was discarded: the machine had a load average of 212 from an unrelated build, and the same gate took 194 s under that load against 105 s without it. Both numbers are published because the first one is what a measurement looks like when nobody checks the load.

No runner-minute savings are claimed. Where CI does run, a local gate reduces the number of red builds, not the number of green ones. Green builds still belong on the runner. The value is a guarantee of feedback, not a speedup.
The tool is not a replacement for CI. It does not test the runner, the matrix, the scheduled jobs, or the deployment. It is a faster answer to 'did I break something?'
The numbers come from one machine and one workspace. They are a starting point for your own measurements, not a benchmark.

findings.headline: What the gate found that the CI could not
findings.body: Found by running the local gate against repositories whose CI was in the state described above. All three were found in under four minutes on a laptop, with no runner minutes spent.

items.title: A stale secret-scan allowlist
items.body: `.gitleaksignore` named `LOCAL_DEVELOPMENT_GUIDE.md`, but the file had moved to `docs/product/LOCAL_DEVELOPMENT_GUIDE.md`. The fingerprint never matched, so a tracked documentation file — a curl sample containing the literal string `YOUR_TOKEN` — was failing the secret scan. The file is tracked, so the CI scan was failing on it too. The CI had been red for the same reason the jobs were not starting, and nobody could tell the two apart.

items.title: Ninety-three dependency advisories
items.body: `npm audit --audit-level=high` is in the workflow. The local gate ran it and it failed: 93 advisories, 53 high, 8 critical. The same command CI runs.

items.title: Build artefacts tripping a working-tree scan
items.body: Playwright traces under `test-results/` contain a token, and a working-tree secret scan reads them. They are build output and belong in the allowlist.

lessons.title: A red build is not always a red build
lessons.body: The instinct on seeing red is to assume your change broke it. The cheapest diagnostic is the timing: six seconds is not a test failure. Six seconds is a job that never started. Reading the annotation instead of the code would have cost ten seconds and saved a week.

lessons.title: Publish the measurement you threw away
lessons.body: The 194-second run under a load average of 212 is in the evidence document. Discarding it silently would have been the normal choice. Publishing it is the reason the 105-second number can be believed at all — a reader knows the spread, and knows the author looked for it.

lessons.title: Green builds still belong on the runner
lessons.body: The honest framing of a local gate is a guarantee, not a replacement. Claiming the local gate is faster would have been false on this hardware, and a single person checking it would have made everything else in the document untrustworthy.

lessons.title: One copy of the setup is the whole trick
lessons.body: Every drift problem I have seen in CI came from two implementations of the same intent. The fix was not a cleverer reconciliation layer. It was deleting one of the two copies and having the Makefile and the workflow call the same files.

caseStudies.title: 250 MB, four processes and a proxy that never settles
caseStudies.subtitle: How one dependency-free Node process replaced four mock containers — and turned the footprint into a build gate instead of a paragraph

hero.headline: Four containers, 250 MB, and a proxy that never settled.
hero.body: The mock environment was a docker compose file with four services. It was slow to start, it idled at nearly 8% CPU, and one of its containers existed to translate OpenAPI specs — and never finished doing it.

problem.headline: The mock environment cost more than the code it was mocking
problem.body:
Every project that talks to a payment gateway, an email provider, an accounting service, a DNS provider, a messaging service or an identity check needs something to talk to in a test. The arrangement in the workspace was four containers: the mock service, an OpenAPI proxy that served the provider specs, and two supporting services.

Measured on one machine with every mock running, that arrangement cost four processes, 250 MB of resident memory, 7.9% idle CPU, and 20 seconds and rising before the first request was answered. 214 MB of the memory and almost all of the CPU belonged to the OpenAPI proxy — the component whose job was translating a spec, and which did not settle.

And the arithmetic was brutal. On a developer laptop, where memory is the scarcest resource, a test setup that permanently occupies a quarter of a gigabyte and never idles is not a tool that gets used often. It is a tool people queue for, postpone, and eventually bypass — which puts the test back to manual, and the manual version back to one senior person who knows how to run it.

The containers were not the problem. The container *count* was the problem, and the runtimes each one dragged in behind it.
problem.pullQuote: A mock environment that costs a quarter of a gigabyte and never idles is not a tool people use often. It is a tool people postpone.
symptoms: Four processes to start, stop and clean up for every test run
250 MB resident with every mock running, of which 214 MB was the OpenAPI proxy alone
7.9% idle CPU while doing nothing, almost all of it in the proxy
20 seconds and rising before the first request was answered
The proxy never settled — it kept translating specs that were already translated

approach.headline: Delete the runtimes until there is nothing left to delete
approach.body:
The rewrite did not add features. It removed everything that could be removed, and then made the result a rule rather than a preference.

The rules are published at the top of the README, because a contributor who breaks one of them breaks the promise in the first line of the file:

**No dependencies.** Not 'few' — none. The engine runs on Node's own HTTP server. A dependency is a package to install, audit and keep out of the advisories.

**No runtime that costs memory to start.** A JVM, a compiled Go binary or a Python environment all add to the footprint before a single request is served. Node is already on the machine, because the project under test runs on it.

**One process for every mock.** Nine mocks in one process cost 50 MB. Nine containers cost nine runtimes.

**In the test, not beside it.** A test that needs a mock starts it in the test process, with `startMock()`. Nothing listens on a port, no container starts, and the mock stops when the test ends. This is the cheapest way to mock anything, and it is why the engine is a library first and a service second.

**Idle means idle.** A mock answers a request and then stops computing. Polling, watching and retrying are how a mock turns into a battery drain.

The last rule is the one most engines get wrong, and it is the reason this one measures 0.0% idle CPU while the stack it replaces sits at 7.9%.
approach.pullQuote2: The last rule is the one most engines get wrong: a mock answers a request and then stops computing.

steps.title: The HTTP core
steps.body: Node's own http module, no framework. Every mock is a route table and a handler, mounted onto one server. This is where the memory floor comes from: there is nothing to load.

steps.title: The provider mocks
steps.body: Eighteen providers — Stripe, Paystack, Interswitch, Flutterwave and Monnify for payments; YouVerify, Smile ID and IdentityPass for identity; Twilio, Termii, OneSignal, WhatsApp and FCM for messaging; Resend, Xero, Cloudflare, OpenAI and S3 for everything else. Every mock answers /health, so a container can be checked without knowing which mock it is.

steps.title: The spec layer
steps.body: Provider contracts are held as OpenAPI documents, with a download script that keeps them current. The spec is the source of truth for a mock's shape, so the mock and the published contract cannot quietly diverge.

steps.title: The control surface
steps.body: A control endpoint and a panel for listing and driving the mocks, so a run can be inspected and reset without restarting the process. This is what makes the engine usable as a service as well as a library.

steps.title: The test integration
steps.body: startMock() runs the mock inside the test process, so nothing listens on a port and nothing needs cleaning up afterwards. The engine is a library first and a service second — that ordering is what makes the footprint claim true in a test run, which is where it matters most.

results.headline: The same work, one fifth of the memory and no idle CPU

before.value: 214 MB, and it does not settle
7.9%, almost all of it the proxy

before.metric: Things to start, stop and clean up

after.metric: Things to start, stop and clean up

notes: The measurement was taken with the project's own `npm run footprint` script, which starts the engine with every mock it carries, waits for the first request to be answered, samples the resident size with `ps`, and samples the CPU with two `ps -o time=` reads ten seconds apart. The container figures come from `docker compose up -d` sampled with `docker stats --no-stream`, once immediately and once after the containers had settled.

The engine's own figures are published as a range rather than a single number, and that is deliberate. The first version of this case study quoted 1.4 s for the first request while the mock engine's evidence document quoted 465 ms for the same measurement. Both were real samples of the same thing on different machines, and the measurement moves by a factor of three depending on what the machine is doing. A single sample presented as *the* figure is not a measurement — it is a number that happened to be true once. Both documents now quote the range and name the script that produces it.

The footprint figures are a build gate, and the gate was repaired rather than merely widened. Its idle budget was 1% over a three-second sampling window, which made it fail two runs in three on an idle machine. A gate that fails sometimes is worse than no gate, because it teaches people to retry it instead of reading it. The window is now ten seconds and the budget 2% — four times above what the engine uses, four times below the 7.9% it exists to catch.

This is a lighter mock, not a faithful sandbox. It answers the calls a test makes. It does not model a provider's business rules, and it is not a staging environment. The documentation says so, in a section of its own.
The footprint was measured when the engine carried nine mocks. It now carries eighteen, and the gate is what keeps the figure honest as that number grows.

governance.headline: The public record is designed so it cannot be inflated
governance.body:
The project publishes a community page with a rule that is unusual and worth stating plainly: the adopter list is a file in the repository, and it grows by pull request. It is public, reviewable, and cannot be inflated — because adding a name requires a commit that anyone can see and revert.

The same page invites press mentions to be submitted as an issue, and states that the list is optional for people who would rather not be named. That is a more credible structure than a testimonials widget, and it is one a reviewer can audit in a minute.

items.title: Adopters live in ADOPTERS.md
items.body: A row is added by pull request. The file is the list. There is no form, no email, no account, and nothing that can be quietly edited.

items.title: Mentions are links, not logos
items.body: Press and mentions are submitted as an issue with a URL. A link can be checked in one click; a logo cannot.

items.title: Listing is optional
items.body: The documentation says outright that being listed is not required, and that the list exists for people who want to be found. Honesty about the absence of a number is worth more than a number nobody can verify.

lessons.title: Footprint decides adoption, not features
lessons.body: The feature set barely moved between the two versions. The footprint moved from 250 MB to 50 MB, and the number of teams that could run it at all moved with it. If the tool will not fit on a laptop, it will not be in the inner loop, and it will not change anyone's behaviour.

lessons.title: 'No dependencies' is a policy, not a preference
lessons.body: Every dependency is a package to install, audit and keep out of the advisories — and this project was already reporting 93 advisories in a different repository. Choosing zero is not asceticism; it is a way of not adding to a problem you are publicly documenting elsewhere.

lessons.title: The rules belong in the README, at the top
lessons.body: The rules are published before the feature list, because the first line of the README is a promise about weight and the rules are what keep it true. A contributor who breaks a rule breaks the promise, and they can see that before they start.

lessons.title: Make the claim a gate
lessons.body: The footprint test fails the build at 100 MB. A number in a README is a claim; a number in a test is a constraint. The difference between the two is the difference between a promise and an enforced property, and it is the same reason the mock engine's 0.0% idle CPU is believable when a competitor's 7.9% is not.

caseStudies.title: Business logic as data, on a host with no internet
caseStudies.subtitle: An air-gapped Windows Service that runs enterprise workflows from JSON blueprints — and records every attempt, including the ones it had to retry

hero.headline: The controller was the problem, not the automation.
hero.body: A platform that can only be extended by editing the thing that runs it will eventually be edited in a hurry, by someone who is not the person who designed it.

problem.headline: Three couplings, each of which is a separate way to lose control
problem.body:
Enterprise automation usually arrives as a controller application. A workflow is a method. Changing a workflow means changing code, which means a build, which means a deploy, which means the change is gated on a pipeline rather than on the person who understands the business rule.

That is the first coupling: **logic and orchestration are tangled together.** A step that shells out to Artifactory and a step that calls Jira live in the same method as the code that decides what runs and in what order, and there is no way to review the first without reading the second.

The second coupling is to the **network**. A controller that calls a cloud AI endpoint to classify an ambiguous request has a hard dependency on somebody else's uptime, and in an air-gapped environment it has none at all. When the endpoint is unreachable, the sensible thing — dropping the transaction, or guessing — are both bad, and the system has to know which one it did.

The third coupling is to the **engine**. Every new integration — Kubernetes, CyberArk, another Artifactory, a tracking system — arrives as an edit to a core module. Core modules accumulate edits. Eventually the core is the thing nobody dares touch, and every integration is a fork of it.

None of these are exotic failures. They are the ordinary, predictable consequence of the shape of the code, and they are all fixable by changing the shape rather than by adding more care.
problem.pullQuote: A workflow that can only be changed by editing the thing that runs it will eventually be edited in a hurry, by someone who is not the person who designed it.
symptoms: Adding a step to a pipeline required a code change, a review and a deployment window
The engine module was edited for every new integration, and had stopped being safe to touch
Retry state lived in memory, so an interrupted run left no recoverable record of what had happened
An unreachable dependency left the platform with no defined behaviour — it either blocked the pipeline or guessed
The audit trail was reconstructed from log text after the fact rather than written as it happened

approach.headline: Three separations, and a defined answer for every failure
approach.body:
**Workflows are data.** A pipeline is a JSON blueprint: a list of steps, each with an identifier, a task, an optional retry count and an input map whose values may interpolate the outputs of earlier steps. It can be diffed, reviewed, approved and replayed without a build. A business rule changes by editing a file, which is the right tool for a business rule.

**The engine core is immutable.** It lives in its own module scope with a composition root that dot-sources the internal components — the database engine, the rules engine, the orchestrator and the router. The engine does not know what any particular workflow does. It knows how to walk a blueprint, resolve an input, run a task, and record the outcome.

**Extensions are discovered, not registered.** A new integration is a file named `*.plugin.ps1` dropped into the plugins directory. It is pure, it takes strict parameters, it does not mutate globals, and it returns dictionaries or hash tables. The engine finds it. The core is never edited.

And for the failure case there is a defined answer rather than a hopeful one. Ambiguous intent is classified by a local model on the host, and if that model is unreachable the classifier falls back to a deterministic regular-expression matrix before dropping the transaction. Either way, the choice made is written to the audit trail — so the system can say not just that it degraded, but exactly which path it took.

architecture.headline: The layout is the argument

steps.title: Immutable engine core
steps.body: Modules/PipelineEngine is a separate module scope with a manifest, a composition root and four internal components: the transactional SQLite database engine, the rules engine that validates and shields against command injection, the orchestrator that resolves variable interpolation and drives the pipeline loop, and the router that performs zero-trust header checks and matches routes by regular expression.

steps.title: Declarative workflow blueprints
steps.body: The workflows directory holds pure JSON — no code, no PowerShell, no side effects at load time. A blueprint declares steps, tasks, inputs and an optional retry count. Because it is data, the same blueprint can be validated by the Pester harness offline, which is what the test suite does with every toggle line.

steps.title: Plug-in auto-discovery
steps.body: The plugins directory is the extension surface. Storage, DevOps and tracking plugins ship as examples, and a new one needs nothing but a file with the right suffix. A plugin that breaks the rules — mutating globals, or returning the wrong shape — is rejected by the contract rather than by convention.

steps.title: Thread-safe shared caches
steps.body: A synchronised hashtable is injected across the runspace pool. The plugin cache compiles script structures on first use and then serves them without touching the filesystem again inside the hot loop. A second, separate cache holds just-in-time secrets generated through the host's DPAPI, with a TTL so a rotated credential cannot outlive its rotation.

steps.title: Transactional persistence and safe backup
steps.body: The database engine writes every step attempt — Retrying, Success or Failed — to SQLite inside a transaction. The backup script performs an online snapshot through SQLite's own backup mechanism, so a copy can be taken without dropping active workers or refusing an inbound webhook.

steps.title: Local-first interface layer
steps.body: The router serves a control console straight out of a public directory on the same socket, with the Vue runtime cached locally rather than pulled from a CDN. There is no build step, no bundler and no node_modules in the deployment — upgrading the console is editing layout tags in a file.

diagram: ├── config.json           settings, feature toggles, RBAC tokens
├── workflows/            pure JSON blueprints (data, not code)
├── tests/                Pester harness — every toggle, offline
└── public/               the control console, served locally

results.headline: What changed, structurally

before.value: An edit to the engine core

after.value: A local model, with a deterministic fallback

notes: No wall-clock benchmark is claimed for this platform, and none should be inferred from one. The claims here are architectural and are checkable by reading the layout: the engine core is a separate module scope, the workflows are data, and the plugins are discovered rather than registered.

The retry policy is explicit. A step declares an optional retryCount, and the delay escalates as 2^(attempt - 1) — two seconds, then four, then eight. Each of those attempts writes its own row, so the audit trail shows the transient failure, the recovery delay and the eventual outcome as three separate facts rather than one summary.

Every cross-cutting concern is a toggle on disk rather than a branch in code: MaintenanceMode returns 503 for executions while leaving the audit read endpoints live, EnableRBAC degrades to a single master token, EnableApprovalGates permits a hotfix to bypass an approval checkpoint, and EnableAIFallback drops an unstructured task rather than guessing. Flipping any of them does not require a restart.
The platform has no external dependencies and no build step. It is registered as a service and it runs — which is the entire point in an environment where the public internet is not available.

governance.headline: The air gap is only as strong as its weakest supply chain
governance.body: A platform that refuses network traffic is only meaningfully air-gapped if the artefacts it runs were verified before they arrived. That is the part of this design most likely to be got wrong, and it is worth being explicit about it.

items.title: A downloader that greps for a keyword is not a verifier
items.body: The asset hydrator fetches the Vue runtime on a connected machine and writes it into the project for transfer to the air-gapped host. If the integrity check is a regular expression over the first line of the downloaded file, then it verifies nothing: it proves a string appears somewhere, not that the bytes are the expected bytes. The check has to be a hash of the whole file against a pinned expected digest, and the digest has to be pinned from a source that is not the same host that served the file.

items.title: Verify the archive, not just the payload
items.body: The right order is: fetch the published artefact, verify the signature or digest of the archive, extract, then verify the extracted file's digest against the version manifest. Checking only the extracted file means the extraction step is trusted blindly.

items.title: Fail with the real reason
items.body: When verification fails, the error must say that the digest did not match the pinned value. A generic 'possible network interception' sends the operator looking at the network, when the network was never the thing at fault.

lessons.title: Configuration is data, not code
lessons.body: Every hour spent moving a business rule out of a controller and into a reviewable file is an hour of the reviewer's attention that used to go to reading code. It is the same lesson as the mock engine's zero-dependency rule, at a different scale: the cheapest thing to review is data, because there is nothing in it that can surprise you.

lessons.title: An extension point that requires editing the core is not an extension point
lessons.body: The plugin directory only works because the engine never learns what a plugin does. The moment a plugin needs something from the core that the core does not already expose, the boundary leaks — and it leaks exactly once, in a hurry, with a deadline.

lessons.title: Define the degraded path before you need it
lessons.body: The local model with a regular-expression fallback was designed as a pair, not as a fallback added later. When the primary path is unavailable, the system already knows what it will do and the audit trail already knows how to record it.

lessons.title: Audit the attempts, not the outcome
lessons.body: Recording only the final state of a retried step erases the information an auditor most wants: that the system hit a transient fault and recovered on its own. Writing one row per attempt is barely more work and turns 'it worked eventually' into a legible sequence.
